references.title: The Four Steps to the Epiphany
references.summary: Customer development: customer discovery, customer validation, customer creation, company building. Discovery and validation search for a repeatable business model; creation and building execute it.

stance.why: Discovery and Validation take Blank's names and meaning.

references.title: Crossing the Chasm
references.summary: The technology adoption life cycle and the chasm between visionaries and pragmatists; cross it by winning one beachhead segment, then neighbouring niches (the bowling alley).

stance.why: Beachhead keeps Moore's meaning: one mainstream segment won outright.

references.title: Inside the Tornado
references.summary: Companion to Crossing the Chasm: the tornado of mass-market adoption and Main Street after it.

stance.why: Scale covers the tornado and Main Street under the common word.

references.title: The only thing that matters (Pmarca Guide to Startups, part 4)
references.summary: Product/market fit means being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market; credits Andy Rachleff. The original blog was taken down and survives on an archive.

stance.why: The Validation gate is product-market fit, tested by retention.

references.title: Repeatability: Build Enduring Businesses for a World of Constant Change
references.summary: Bain study of 200+ companies: enduring growth comes from a repeatable business model; complexity is a silent killer of profitable growth.

stance.why: The Beachhead gate is repeatability.

references.title: The Alchemy of Growth
references.summary: McKinsey's three horizons: H1 extend the core, H2 build emerging businesses, H3 create options. The horizons run at the same time, as a portfolio.

stance.why: Used as a lens, not as phase names, because its horizons are concurrent rather than sequential.

references.title: Expanded six-phase milestone framework (Discovery, Validation, Retention, Repeatability, Scale, Platformization)
authors: Google (AI assistant conversation shared by the founder)
references.summary: A synthesized six-phase model separating retention (product-market fit) and repeatability from validation and scale. No published source.

stance.why: Retention and repeatability became gates rather than phases; Platformization became Platform.

references.title: The thin edge of the wedge strategy
references.summary: Enter a market with a narrow product or segment that solves an acute problem, then expand from that foothold; related to the bowling-pin strategy.

stance.why: Wedge is a portfolio role with this meaning, not a phase.

references.title: Defining the Business: The Starting Point of Strategic Planning
references.summary: A business is defined on three dimensions: customer groups (who), customer functions (what need), and technologies (how).

stance.why: Market, job and technology on each product card.

references.title: North American Industry Classification System 2022
references.summary: Production-oriented industry classification: 20 sectors, six-digit codes; establishments with similar production processes share an industry.

stance.why: Industry codes use NAICS.

references.title: Global Industry Classification Standard
references.summary: Market-oriented industry classification used by investors.

stance.why: Kept as an alternative system; NAICS is the default.

references.title: Treasury Regulation 1.183-2: activity not engaged in for profit
references.summary: Nine factors for whether an activity is a business or a hobby; an activity profitable in 3 of 5 years is presumed for profit.

stance.why: hobby is the first value of ambition, in the IRS sense.

references.title: What Do Entrepreneurs Create?
references.summary: Four venture types: survival, lifestyle, managed growth, aggressive growth; ventures rarely change type, and a portfolio should balance types.

stance.why: The remaining ambition values.

references.title: The Business Model Navigator
references.summary: 55 recurring business model patterns from the University of St. Gallen; a business model answers who, what, how and how revenue is realized.

stance.why: business_model values are the Navigator's pattern names.

references.title: The Core Competence of the Corporation
references.summary: A core competence is collective learning that gives access to many markets, adds to perceived customer benefit and is hard to imitate; core products embody it.

stance.why: The core product's competence field.

references.title: Principles of Marketing: the three levels of product
references.summary: A product has levels: the core customer benefit, the actual product, and the augmented product.

stance.why: The core promise is the core benefit stated as what anyone can claim from the venture.

references.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 Software, systems and enterprise: Architecture description
references.summary: An architecture description describes a system through models; a view is the result of applying a viewpoint, which names the stakeholders' concerns and the model kinds that answer them, to the system. One model can take part in many views.

stance.why: The Venture Anatomy Matrix is the venture's architecture description: each sub-matrix is a model, and the Lean Canvas, Business Model Canvas and an S-1 outline are views produced by viewpoints (EE-157).

references.title: ISO/IEC 9075-2:2011 (SQL:2011) temporal features: application-time and system-versioned tables
references.summary: Application time (valid time) records when a fact holds in the world; system time (transaction time) records when the database held it. Using both gives bitemporal tables, and the two times are independent.

stance.why: Each anatomy cell carries application time (valid_from, valid_to); system time is the provenance log and blob store, so the matrix answers both what we believed at t and what was true at t (EE-157).

references.title: Temporal database (overview of valid time, transaction time and bitemporal data)
references.summary: Secondary overview of temporal database concepts and the TSQL2 and SQL:2011 lineage.

stance.why: Background for the bitemporal terms used in EE-157.

references.title: View model (overview of views and viewpoints, IEEE 1471 lineage)
references.summary: Secondary overview: a viewpoint specifies concerns and modelling techniques; a view is that viewpoint applied to a system.

stance.why: Background for ISO 42010's terms as used in EE-157.

references.title: The Business Model Ontology: A Proposition in a Design Science Approach
references.summary: PhD thesis, University of Lausanne: nine building blocks (value proposition, target customer, distribution channel, relationship, value configuration, capability, partnership, cost structure, revenue model), later the Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder and Pigneur, Business Model Generation, 2010).

stance.why: Too narrow to be the whole venture model; kept as one view over the matrix (EE-157).

references.title: A Guide to the Business Architecture Body of Knowledge (BIZBOK Guide), version 15
references.summary: Business architecture through four core maps (capability, value stream, information, organization) assembled into blueprints for different audiences. A body of knowledge, not a formal standard.

stance.why: Built for large enterprises; its blueprint idea matches views, but ISO 42010 is the formal standard (EE-157).

references.title: Digital twin of an organization
references.summary: A dynamic model of the organization fed by operational and contextual data, used to plan, monitor and simulate. An analyst term, not a standard.

stance.why: Describes the ambition of a live venture model; not adopted as a name because it is a vendor and analyst term (EE-157).

references.title: Regulation S-K (17 CFR part 229), with Form S-1
references.summary: What a registration statement such as Form S-1 must disclose besides financial statements (Regulation S-X): Item 101 description of business, 105 risk factors, 303 management's discussion and analysis, 401 directors and officers, 403 security ownership. Items 101, 103 and 105 were modernized in 2020 (Release 33-10825).

stance.why: The coverage check for the Venture Anatomy Matrix: every S-K item a company would disclose maps to at least one sub-matrix (EE-157).

references.title: Form S-1 registration statement
references.summary: The registration statement for an initial public offering; Part I is the prospectus. Content follows Regulation S-K and S-X.

stance.why: An S-1-style outline is one view over the matrix (EE-157).

references.title: Modernization of Regulation S-K Items 101, 103 and 105: Small Entity Compliance Guide
references.summary: The 2020 amendments: risk factors are material factors, organized under headings, with a summary when long.

stance.why: Shapes the risk sub-matrix (EE-157).

references.title: How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy
references.summary: Harvard Business Review: industry structure through five forces, supplier power, buyer power, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes and rivalry among existing competitors.

stance.why: The industry anatomy matrix rates the five forces low, medium or high (EE-157).

references.title: A General Model for Understanding Organizational Buying Behavior
references.summary: Journal of Marketing 36(2): organizational purchases are made by a buying center of several roles (users, influencers, buyers, deciders, gatekeepers).

stance.why: The market cell buying_roles counts the roles in the buying center; three or more means interviews must span roles (EE-157).

references.title: Merger Guidelines (2023)
references.summary: Issued December 18, 2023. A market with an HHI over 1,800 is highly concentrated (the 2010 Horizontal Merger Guidelines had used 2,500).

stance.why: The market cell concentration uses the 2023 bands: under 1,000 fragmented, 1,000 to 1,800 moderate, over 1,800 concentrated (EE-157).

references.title: Clockspeed: Winning Industry Control in the Age of Temporary Advantage
references.summary: Industries evolve at different clockspeeds, the rate at which products, processes and organizations change; fast-clockspeed industries need shorter planning and evidence horizons.

stance.why: The industry cell clockspeed; fast clockspeed shortens how long evidence stays fresh, 9 months instead of 18 (EE-157).

references.title: Exploit the Product Life Cycle
references.summary: Harvard Business Review: markets and products pass through introduction, growth, maturity and decline, each needing different strategy.

stance.why: The market cell maturity uses emerging, growth, mature and declining (EE-157).

references.title: The Startup Owner's Manual
references.summary: Customer development step by step, including market sizing as total, served and target market (TAM, SAM, SOM).

stance.why: Naive counts the obtainable market as reachable buyers (a head count) as well as dollars, because gate thresholds scale with how many people can be reached (EE-157).

references.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Systems and software engineering: Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering
references.summary: The processes and products of requirements engineering: eliciting stakeholder needs, writing each requirement so it is necessary, unambiguous, verifiable and traceable, and the content of the stakeholder, system and software requirements specifications.

stance.why: Naive's requirements engineer works to it (EE-238): each requirement record says what it serves and how it is verified, and the requirements-spec document kind renders them as a specification.

references.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 26514:2022 Systems and software engineering: Design and development of information for users
references.summary: How information for the users of a system is designed and developed: knowing the audience and its tasks, structuring topics by kind, keeping the information accurate against the system it describes, and reviewing and testing it before release.

stance.why: Naive's technical writer and instruction steward work to it (EE-238): a docs page reads its facts from records and says where none exist, and the instructions agents read are kept true against the code.

references.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 Systems and software engineering: Software life cycle processes
references.summary: The processes of a software life cycle, among them configuration management, which identifies, records and releases baselines, and transition, which moves a release into use.

stance.why: Naive's release manager works to its configuration management and transition processes (EE-238): a release records what was frozen into it, and production ship stays a person's decision.
